claims.claim: Evagrius Ponticus was a Christian monk and former deacon/archdeacon who lived from about 345/346 to 399 AD.
He was born in Ibora in the Roman province of Pontus (modern Turkey) and later served in Constantinople before retreating to Jerusalem and then the Egyptian desert.
The work "Sententiae ad virginem" (Exhortation to a Virgin) consists of fifty‑six short sayings written in distichs that imitate the style of Proverbs.
The sayings are addressed to an unnamed virgin who is probably an associate of the ascetic patrons Melania the Elder and Rufinus of Aquileia.
Its purpose is to give spiritual instruction and practical guidance for the monastic life of women, functioning in some ways as a rule.
The work survives in several medieval Latin manuscripts, including Vatican Reg. lat. 140 (9th c.), Rome BNC 1348 (after 816), Paris lat. 239 (10th‑11th c.) and Toulouse 162 (12th c.).
In the Roman manuscript tradition the work was at times transmitted as part of the “Institutio Sanctimonialium” and was even ascribed to Augustine of Hippo.
Scholars often associate the Sententiae with Evagrius’s larger collection “The Mirrors” (CPG 2435) and study it as an early example of a monastic rule for women.
